### Problem: Rotate image {#sec-mat-p2-rotate}

::: {.p-statement}
Rotate an $n \times n$ matrix by $90^\circ$ clockwise **in place** — modify the input directly, do not return a new matrix.

$1 \le n \le 20$, cells are integers. `[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]` becomes `[[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]]`. `[[5,1,9,11],[2,4,8,10],[13,3,6,7],[15,14,12,16]]` becomes `[[15,13,2,5],[14,3,4,1],[12,6,8,9],[16,7,10,11]]`.

Source: [LC 48 · Rotate Image](https://leetcode.com/problems/rotate-image/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A $90^\circ$ clockwise turn sends cell $(i, j)$ to $(j, n-1-i)$. Read that map as "transpose $(i,j) \to (j,i)$, then reverse each row $(j,i) \to (j, n-1-i)$" and you get two cheap in-place passes; read it as a cycle of four positions and you rotate each four-cell orbit directly.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Copy with the rotation formula.** Write `new[j][n-1-i] = a[i][j]` into a fresh grid and copy it back. Easiest to prove, $O(n^2)$ extra memory.
2. **Transpose, then reverse rows.** Swap across the main diagonal (only the strict upper triangle, $j > i$), then reverse every row. Two passes, each obviously correct, $O(1)$ extra memory.
3. **Four-cycle in place.** The map is the cycle $(i,j) \to (j,n-1-i) \to (n-1-i,n-1-j) \to (n-1-j,i) \to (i,j)$. Every cell lies in exactly one such orbit of four cells, except the centre of an odd grid, which is an orbit of one. For ring $i < n/2$ and $j = i \dots n-2-i$, move the four values one step around their orbit with one temporary.

**Invariant.** In the four-cycle form, after processing representative $(i,j)$ its whole orbit holds its final values, and no later step touches that orbit again: the representatives $i < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, $i \le j < n-1-i$ pick each orbit exactly once.
:::

::: {#fig-mat-p2-rotate}

```{python}

           [["1", "2", "3"],
            ["4", "5", "6"],

           colors={(0, 0): "green", (0, 2): "cyan", (2, 2): "amber", (2, 0): "pink",
                   (1, 1): "muted"},
           cell_w=0.95, size=11)
    V.text(ax, p, 3.15, 1.5, "90 CW", color="muted")
    V.arrow(ax, p, 2.6, 1.5, 3.0, 1.5, color="muted")
```

The corner four-cycle $1 \to 3 \to 9 \to 7 \to 1$ (green/cyan/amber/pink) and the fixed centre (muted). The same colours track where each corner lands after the turn.

:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Copy with the rotation formula

::: {.form-next}
One grid in, one grid out: `new[j][n-1-i] = a[i][j]` for every cell. You then copy `new` back over `a` to satisfy the in-place contract. $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n^2)$ extra space, and there is no swapping logic to reason about — the safest first rung and the reference every other rung is stress-tested against.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("rotate", "formula")
    assert str(final) == "[[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def rotate_copy(a):
    n = len(a)
    new = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            new[j][n - 1 - i] = a[i][j]
    for i in range(n):
        a[i] = new[i][:]
    return a


assert rotate_copy([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]) == [[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]
assert rotate_copy([[5, 1, 9, 11], [2, 4, 8, 10], [13, 3, 6, 7], [15, 14, 12, 16]]) == \
    [[15, 13, 2, 5], [14, 3, 4, 1], [12, 6, 8, 9], [16, 7, 10, 11]]
assert rotate_copy([[1]]) == [[1]]
```

##### C++

```cpp
void rotateCopy(vector<vector<int>>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    vector<vector<int>> nw(n, vector<int>(n));
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)
            nw[j][n - 1 - i] = a[i][j];
    a = nw;
}
```

:::

#### Transpose, then reverse rows

::: {.form-next}
Two passes, $O(1)$ extra space. Transpose over the main diagonal (`swap a[i][j] <-> a[j][i]` for $j > i$ only — swapping the whole grid transposes twice and undoes it), then reverse each row. This is the decomposition with the cleanest correctness proof: composition of two obviously-correct involutions.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("rotate", "extra")
    assert str(final) == "[[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def rotate_trend(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            a[i][j], a[j][i] = a[j][i], a[i][j]
    for row in a:
        row.reverse()
    return a


assert rotate_trend([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]) == [[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]
assert rotate_trend([[5, 1, 9, 11], [2, 4, 8, 10], [13, 3, 6, 7], [15, 14, 12, 16]]) == \
    [[15, 13, 2, 5], [14, 3, 4, 1], [12, 6, 8, 9], [16, 7, 10, 11]]
for _ in range(50):
    n = random.randint(1, 6)
    M = [[a * n + b for b in range(n)] for a in range(n)]
    assert rotate_trend([row[:] for row in M]) == rotate_copy([row[:] for row in M])
```

##### C++

```cpp
void rotateTrend(vector<vector<int>>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
            swap(a[i][j], a[j][i]);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        reverse(a[i].begin(), a[i].end());
}
```

:::

#### Four-cycle in place

::: {.form-next}
Rotate each four-cell orbit with one simultaneous assignment (a tuple rotation in Python, one `temp` and four writes in C++), walking $j$ along the top edge of every ring. Only the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ rings and, within ring $i$, only the first $n - 1 - 2i$ cells of its top edge are visited — the other three cells of each orbit are moved by the same statement. $O(1)$ space, and each cell is written exactly once.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("rotate", "cycle")
    assert str(final) == "[[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def rotate_cycle(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n // 2):
        for j in range(i, n - 1 - i):
            a[i][j], a[j][n - 1 - i], a[n - 1 - i][n - 1 - j], a[n - 1 - j][i] = \
                a[n - 1 - j][i], a[i][j], a[j][n - 1 - i], a[n - 1 - i][n - 1 - j]
    return a


assert rotate_cycle([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]) == [[7, 4, 1], [8, 5, 2], [9, 6, 3]]
assert rotate_cycle([[5, 1, 9, 11], [2, 4, 8, 10], [13, 3, 6, 7], [15, 14, 12, 16]]) == \
    [[15, 13, 2, 5], [14, 3, 4, 1], [12, 6, 8, 9], [16, 7, 10, 11]]
assert rotate_cycle([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) == [[3, 1], [4, 2]]
for _ in range(50):
    n = random.randint(1, 6)
    M = [[a * n + b for b in range(n)] for a in range(n)]
    assert rotate_cycle([row[:] for row in M]) == rotate_copy([row[:] for row in M])
```

##### C++

```cpp
void rotateCycle(vector<vector<int>>& a) {
    int n = a.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n / 2; ++i) {
        for (int j = i; j < n - 1 - i; ++j) {
            int temp = a[i][j];
            a[i][j] = a[n - 1 - j][i];
            a[n - 1 - j][i] = a[n - 1 - i][n - 1 - j];
            a[n - 1 - i][n - 1 - j] = a[j][n - 1 - i];
            a[j][n - 1 - i] = temp;
        }
    }
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
All three are $\Theta(n^2)$ time. **Copy** uses $\Theta(n^2)$ extra space; **transpose+reverse** and **four-cycle** are $\Theta(1)$ extra. The **four-cycle** writes each cell once ($\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ orbit rotations); **transpose+reverse** writes most cells twice but is the easiest to prove correct, and the copy form is the oracle both are stress-tested against.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 1$: nothing moves; every rung returns the single element.
- $n = 2$: one orbit of $4$, `[[1,2],[3,4]] -> [[3,1],[4,2]]`.
- Odd $n$: the exact centre is an orbit of size $1$ and is correctly skipped, because the ring loop only visits $i < n/2$ and $j$ stops before the far corner.
- Counter-clockwise $90^\circ$: transpose, then reverse the *order of the rows* (equivalently reverse each row first, then transpose), or run the four-cycle in the other direction. Careful: reversing the order of the rows *first* and then transposing is the **clockwise** turn again.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Transposing the full grid.** Looping `for i in range(n): for j in range(n): swap(a[i][j],a[j][i])` swaps each pair twice and leaves the matrix unchanged. Transpose only the strict upper triangle (`j` from `i+1`).
- **Reversing columns instead of rows.** Transpose + reverse-**rows** is clockwise; transpose + reverse-**columns** is counter-clockwise — a classic sign error on the wrong sample.
- **Four-cycle writes in the wrong order.** The target `a[j][n-1-i]` must be read before it is overwritten; the tuple assignment (Python) or a single `temp` held across all four writes (C++) is what keeps the reads fresh.
:::

**Variants.** Transpose Matrix (@sec-mat-p2-transpose) is the transpose half on its own, on a possibly non-square input where in-place stops working. [LC 1886 · Determine Whether Matrix Can Be Obtained By Rotation](https://leetcode.com/problems/determine-whether-matrix-can-be-obtained-by-rotation/){difficulty="Easy"} asks which of the four rotations maps one grid onto another. Rotating by $180^\circ$ is two clockwise turns, or simply reversing the order of the rows and then every row.

**Try it.** Rotate clockwise by *reverse-then-transpose*: reverse the order of the rows, then transpose, and prove with the index formulas that it equals transpose-then-reverse-each-row.
